initial_observation.encounter_context: referred to the otolaryngology clinic for further management of aggressive left glomus jugulare
initial_observation.chief_complaint: left ear discharge associated with decreased hearing and non-pulsatile tinnitus
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: The patient complained of left ear discharge associated with decreased hearing and non-pulsatile tinnitus persisting for four months; known to have chronic kidney disease on hemodialysis, history of stroke resulting in left facial palsy and hemiparesis; no history of otalgia, aural fullness, or vertigo
known_prior_history: history of stroke with left facial palsy and hemiparesis

evidence_items.source_text: Clinical examination of the left ear revealed a central wet tympanic membrane perforation with mildly congested middle ear mucosa. Except for the central facial palsy, the right ear and other structures examined, including the cranial nerves, were intact.
Audiological assessment revealed left conductive hearing loss.
Flexible nasopharyngoscopy revealed a bulge in the left nasopharyngeal wall, but no obvious mass was observed.
Her ear infection resolved after a course of oral and topical ciprofloxacin.

Computed tomography (CT) of the temporal bone revealed a large mass of mixed density with cystic and solid components. It was ill-defined and infiltrative and had an extensively enhancing component extending to the left petrous apex and left side of the clivus. There was an inferior extension to the left infratemporal fossa and nasopharyngeal and parapharyngeal spaces, displacing the nasopharynx anteriorly with adjacent airway narrowing without mucosal invasion. The lesion extended to the left mastoid air cells and middle ear cavity. It infiltrated the left jugular bulb and inferiorly extended to the proximal jugular vein with non-opacification, invasion, and significant osseous destruction of the left petrous bone and occipital condyle. Dehiscence, left carotid canal resorption, and left jugular foramen widening were also observed (Fig. 1, Fig. 2).

Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a large heterogeneous mixed cystic and soft tissue lesion extending to the left petrous apex (Fig. 3). The cystic component showed high signal intensity on T2 and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images (Fig. 3A, B). The soft tissue component showed an isointense signal in all sequences without diffusion restriction.

The cystic component showed high signal intensity on T2 and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images (Fig. 3A, B). The soft tissue component showed an isointense signal in all sequences without diffusion restriction.
In our case, the diffusion-weighted imaging sequence demonstrated hypointensity of the aneurysm, whereas the apparent diffusion coefficient sequence showed hyperattenuation.
Diagnostic CT angiography revealed a left dissection aneurysm in the petrous part of the ICA (Fig. 4).

Stenting of the petrous part of the ICA was performed. Wall opposition was also improved with carotid angioplasty using a hyperglide balloon. The procedure was successful with satisfactory deployment of the construct, clear flow diversion away from the aneurysm, and desirable stagnation within the aneurysm (Fig. 5).

However, she was administered several antibiotics, and she developed herpes zoster with altered consciousness during admission. She started to gradually regain consciousness and was discharged on daily aspirin and clopidogrel when she was stable.

dissection aneurysm in the petrous part of the ICA
